From Old Galician-Portuguese ser, from Early Medieval Latin essere, from Latin esse. The forms sou (“I am”) and sois pl (“you are”) derive from a Vulgar Latin *sonō and *sutis.
Along the way, the verb absorbed Old Galician-Portuguese seer < Latin sedēre (“sit”). The latter supplied the present subjunctive of modern ser, where /-ʒ-/ reflects Late Latin /-(d)j-/, as in seja < sedeat).

examples.english: Needless to say, dinner was a real disaster: it had stone-hard, “united we'll win”-type rice, and “shoe sole”-like meat; the salad was sort of spared, even then because Claudia didn't want to comment anything regarding a slug she saw on the ill-washed lettuce. But there did the saying “hunger is the best seasoning” fit perfectly.
examples.ref: 2008, Priscila Ferraz, nuvem de pó [powdercloud], Marco Zero, →ISBN, page 58:
examples.text: Nem é preciso dizer que o jantar foi um verdadeiro desastre. Mas ali coube perfeitamente o dito popular “a fome é o melhor tempero”.
